speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: asked the Prime Minister in light of the tighter monetary policy stance taken by MAS (a) what is the projected impact on our trade exports from the strengthening of the Singapore dollar; (b) how will the Government ensure that the strengthened Singapore dollar does not adversely impact our export competitiveness in the long run; and (c) whether the Ministry will continue to strengthen the Singapore dollar if core inflation does not moderate over the next few months.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The Monetary Authority of Singapore's (MAS) monetary policy is aimed at keeping inflation low, especially over the medium term.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Achieving low inflation also supports sustained economic growth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS seeks to achieve this through an exchange rate-centred monetary policy, in particular, by managing the Singapore dollar against a basket of currencies of Singapore's major trading partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: When inflationary pressures build up, MAS allows the trade-weighted exchange rate to appreciate faster, thereby helping to reduce imported inflation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This has been in line with rising global price pressures and the improvement in external economic conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The strengthening of the Singapore dollar is necessary to dampen inflation and to help preserve the purchasing power of businesses and households.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It is not expected to have a significant negative impact on Singapore's exports.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Growth in non-oil domestic exports has remained firm in Q1 2022.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: With continuing uncertainty in the global economic environment, Singapore's exports are, primarily, dependent on demand rather than our exchange rate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This is borne out in EDB's latest survey of Business Expectations of the Manufacturing Sector, which showed that the Singapore dollar exchange rate is not a key limiting factor for manufacturing firms' export orders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Singapore's exports are, generally, high value-added products and services where demand is less sensitive to price and, therefore, exchange rate changes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Further, a stronger exchange rate helps reduce the import costs faced by our export industries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Inflation is, however, expected to remain at elevated rates for some time, higher than what we have experienced in recent years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This has, primarily, been due to pressures in global energy and other commodity markets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: However, because MAS began shifting its policy stance early, it has been able to respond to rising inflationary pressure through gradual shifts in exchange rate policy, including in its latest April Monetary Policy Statement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Had MAS not begun tightening policy last year, ahead of many central banks, it would have had to allow for a steeper appreciation of the exchange rate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS' monetary policy response is also part of the Government's multi-pronged strategy to deal with rising inflationary pressures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: As Members know, the Government has set aside considerable resources to help Singapore businesses, especially SMEs, and our households cope with higher costs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: One, how does MAS expect the strengthening of the Singapore dollar to affect Singapore's GDP forecast for the year?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Two, the tightening effects of our monetary policy are, eventually, relative to what other countries have similarly done.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: So, how has the surge in the US dollar dampened the effects of the measures to tighten or strengthen the Singapore dollar, and if so, will further measures be needed?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And MAS' monetary policy stance is consistent with the macroeconomic outcome of GDP growth within this forecast range.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As I have mentioned in my original answer, MAS manages the Singapore dollar against a basket of currencies of Singapore's major trading partners, within the policy band.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, any bilateral exchange rate movement will, accordingly, have a more muted impact on the Singapore dollar's effective exchange rate, which remains in line with MAS' monetary policy stance, as announced in April.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But MAS will continue to focus on medium-term price stability and avoid sudden large shifts in policy and, in aggregate, will remain vigilant to developments in the external environment and their impact on the Singapore economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I wonder, in light of what he shared about how MAS has allowed three separate adjustments to the band since last year, I would note that the Singapore dollar has only appreciated, depending on how one measures it – between 1.5% and about 2.7% or 2.8% since then.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, inflation rates are significantly higher than that.
